As in the title, I've been involved in the pipeline construction world for 4 years now, with an additional 4 years in other areas of the oil patch in Alberta. I specialize in industrial coatings and corrosion. I can answer most any question you have about oil and natural gas pipeline construction. If I don't have the answer, I can send a text message to one of my colleagues and get an answer!

Pipelining can be a grueling job. You work on a project basis for weeks at a time, sometimes running 7 days a week with very few days off. Some of the locations I've worked have been very remote requiring us to set up work camps in the middle of forests. Other times I'm going right through your back yard!

Pipeline has had bad rap lately due to Keystone and all that jazz. I'm hoping y'all can see that we're just folks trying to make a living like anyone else.

"There ain't nothing finer than a rich pipeliner digging ditches for his bitches back home"
So You Wanna Be A Pipeliner? (I am a Oil and Gas Pipeline Construction Foreman, AMA)

1. Do you ever have any qualms about directly enabling a nonrenewable resource to pollute the planet just so you and the company you work for can make a buck, when alternative forms of energy are both available and as profitable?

  2. Have you ever considered learning more about the renewable energy industry? I ask this one because I'm of the opinion that if the US funded the retraining of oil industry workers, that not only would a sustainable energy infrastructure be both supported and boosted, but no jobs would be lost, and best-case scenario, more jobs would be created. Thoughts?
If I wanted to be a pipe fitter or plumber, what would I need to learn?

For plumbing it would be tech school and placement with a plumbing company.

Not many apprentices come through the old way anymore.

I suggest you check the job section for apprentice positions or contact your local tech school (they can help find a job placement)
This might be a dumb question but would I have to join a union to get a job after tech school? How easy / hard is it to get a job if you aren't a member of a union?

I'm in Australia so things are no doubt much different here.

My city is largely union free, but in some places the unions have tight control of who works where.

If you go the apprenticeship route your company will enrol you in the union and take care of that end.

I'm pretty happy to be away from it tbh, our local union has done good things, but they are regarded as bully boys (I've also seen this first hand)
Thanks. I'm in the US and I don't really know much about unions or how to deal with them.

All good mate..

Keep in mind that they are there for your rights at work. In Australia they have helped workers beyond [belief(]http://www.australianunions.org.au/union_achievements) but at the same time the construction/mining/forestry union has so much power that backhanders and corruption are inevitable.

Good luck with your career mate! Il also suggest you take as many courses, modules and training opportunities as you can..

Trades work is frickin hard and extra knowledge means it is easier for you to find a cosy management position when your older!!
